stemMd: A cafe can serve either soup or sandwiches at lunch, but not both. The owner says soup is the better choice because each serving yields a positive profit greater than the profit on a sandwich. Which assumption would make the reasoning sufficient?

options.label: B
options.textMd: A positive number of soup servings would be sold, at least as many as the number of sandwiches that would be sold, with no other difference in daily costs.

options.label: C
options.textMd: Sandwiches can be eaten without cutlery.

options.label: D
options.textMd: The cafe has served sandwiches before.

explanationMd: Compare daily profit, not just unit margin. Let the positive soup margin be p and sandwich margin q, with p>q. The added assumption gives soup quantity S>0 and S at least sandwich quantity N. If q is nonnegative, pS>qS>=qN; if q is negative, positive soup profit exceeds the nonpositive sandwich contribution. Equal other costs therefore make soup strictly more profitable.

distractorRationale.d: Prior experience does not compare future daily profits.
distractorRationale.e: This could reduce sales or increase costs rather than justify the choice.
distractorRationale.c: That feature does not determine total profit.
distractorRationale.a: Some preference does not establish enough sales.
